meta.note: Story is DATA. v3 = Hero's Road rugged arm + the Raggeth finale. Post 4 is now a real 2-way PHYSICAL fork (path gentle/rugged) — old wisp death-trap + wrong-turn failsafe retired; Cleverness is earned at the fork on BOTH arms. Rugged arm = posts r1..r5 (fairy spring gives have_water; gentle arm has no spring -> no water). The pond (wp7) is the LAST QR; choosing 'go end Raggeth' starts the Road to Raggeth: gateless (no-QR) tap-through waypoints rg_* the walker advances with 'Walk on' while following red tree-arrows on foot. Cauldron puzzle: cast 3 caps, then quench — water => Crown Reborn (clean), no water => Pyrrhic; wrong/incomplete attempts use `retry` choices that flare + (escalating) hint and never dead-end. PAWN versions of the rugged arm and the finale are NOT written — see the `[PAWN — not yet written]` stubs. DRAFT prose throughout the new Hero content; escalating cauldron hint text is placeholder (owner to finalize). Render order per scene: text -> choice result -> seasonalIntro -> textCont -> variant -> endingVariant (only after choices settle AND the chosen choice has no `next`) -> textAfter. A waypoint may hold `scenes` (pinned on first entry, picked by `when`), each with its OWN text/prompt/choices/next/wayfinding. A choice may carry `next` (advance, overrides scene next), `advanceLabel` (custom continue button), `retry` (puzzle: flare + hint, no advance; optional `hints` array escalates), or `ending`. `gateless:true` = advanced to by an in-app button, not a QR scan.

voices.fox: The Fox (a thread of a voice, then warm)
voices.knight: The Stone Knight / dead captain (vast, grief-worn)

crown.title: The Crown of the Mushroom King
crown.blurb: A shadowed wood, for the brave.

wp1.title: The Entrance
wp1.text:
A moth settles on the post beside you, its light guttering like a candle in a draft. “Traveler. Come close — closer, while my light still holds.” With every word the glow fades a little more. “I am the last of King Bolete’s messengers. The others, Lord Raggeth caught and snuffed out, one by one. I have flown a long way to find you, and I have not much left to burn.”

Behind it, the wood is wrong — grey, too silent, the smell of rot on the cold air.

“The king is dying. His crown is a ring of golden mushroom-caps — for what else would a mushroom-king wear? — and Lord Raggeth crept into the castle and tore three of those caps away. Where the crown goes dark, the forest follows. You can feel it already — the cold, the silence, the rot creeping root to root. By the last bell of nightfall the king’s heart will stop, and this wood will be Raggeth’s to rule: a kingdom of ash and bone. Three caps, scattered through the dark. Find them. Mend the crown. It is the only way left.”

It presses something small into your hand. “A honey-cake. There is little kindness left in this wood, traveler — spend yours well. It may cost more than you think. Go now. And trust no light but mine.”

wp2.title: Into the Forest
wp2.text:
You step off the road and the wood closes behind you like a held breath. The trees here are sick — bark gone black and weeping, leaves curled to ash. A small bird lies still in the path; the moth’s light passes over it and moves on, and does not look.

And the trees have faces — had you not noticed? Look again, as you walk. In the bark of the old ones: faces. Eyes and mouths and furrowed brows, watching you pass. “The forest’s old sentinels,” the moth says softly. “Awake since the first acorn fell. Once they sang to every traveler who came this way. But the king is dying, and one by one they have gone silent and still, their eyes drifting shut. They watch you now without a sound.”

The moth gathers what light it has, and tells you plainly what waits ahead, so you cannot say you were not warned:

“There are lights in this wood that wear a kind voice and a kind face, and they lead only to the bone-fields. There is a rot that spreads by touch and never, ever stops — it is the king’s dying, made into a thing that crawls. There are dead who do not rest, who guard to the grave what they died for. And there is Raggeth himself — who does not always kill what he catches. Sometimes he keeps it. Sometimes he turns it, and sends it back wearing your own face.”

Far off, a bell tolls — slow, and then slower. “The king’s heart,” the moth murmurs. “Hear how it fails. Three caps: one lies where a dying friend keeps watch, one where a false light feeds, one among the dead who were never avenged. This is the road ahead, traveler. It does not get kinder than here.”
wp2.prompt: Commit to the road ahead, or turn back?

choices.label: Go on into the dark
choices.text: You set your jaw and follow the leaning, half-rotted signpost deeper in. The moth’s light steadies, just a little, as if glad of company.

choices.label: Turn back — this is not my fight
choices.text: You turn for the road, and the daylight, and home. The moth does not plead. It only dims. Behind you, as you go, the last of its light gutters out, and the wood draws its silence closed over the king, and over the fox who waited, and over the dead who were never avenged. By morning there is no forest here at all — only ash, and bone, and a cold that came to stay. You were the last one it sent for.

wp3.title: The Great Old Tree
wp3.text:
Beneath the oldest tree, in the last patch the rot has not yet reached, a fox with one silver eye lies in the leaves. He is little more than bone and grey fur, and his breath comes shallow. He has guarded this place since before the tree stood tall — and now he is starving, for the blight has killed everything he might have hunted.

“I cannot move,” he says, and his voice is a thread. “I have not eaten in a week. I will not last the night.” Your hand finds the honey-cake. It is the only food you carry, and the night is long. This is the choice that sets your road.
wp3.prompt: Give him the honey-cake, or keep it?

choices.label: Give the honey-cake
choices.text: He eats slowly, gratefully, and when he is done his silver eye kindles like a struck coin. Strength returns to him by degrees. “Kindness,” he says softly, “is the first gold — rarer in this wood than any crown. You spent it on a dying old fox when you might have kept it for yourself.” From the moss he lifts a small golden cap and lays it in your palm. “I will not forget. When the dark is deepest, and every other light has failed you — look for my eye.” He rises, unsteady but alive, and slips into the shadows ahead, going before you. You will not walk this wood alone. This is the Hero’s Road.

choices.label: Keep it for yourself
choices.text:
You close your hand around the honey-cake and step around him. The fox says nothing — only watches you pass with his one silver eye, and you feel that eye on your back long after the trees have hidden him. There, in the leaves where he lies, the first golden cap gleams; it was the king’s, and the fox had no strength left to guard it. You lift it. Behind you, the old fox lowers his head to the cold ground. He will not see the morning.

And something in the wood feels the cruelty of it — a small coldness, given freely, in a place starved of warmth. Far off, in the deep of the trees, something that had been sleeping opens its eyes and turns, slow and pleased, toward you. You have opened a door. This is the Pawn’s Road.

scenes.text:
The path forks at a leaning, half-rotted post — and this time there is no lying light, no lure, no trick. Just two honest ways to the same far pond. To your right the trail bends away gentle and even, winding off through the trees on level ground. Straight ahead it pitches down into a dark hollow — stony, steep, and far longer, the harder of the two by a long mile.

“Two roads, and both of them true,” the moth says, hovering close. “The right-hand way is kinder to your legs and quicker to the king. The straight way drops into the low ground — steeper, longer, thick with his biting flies; but the king’s oldest friends keep to it, and there are gifts on it found nowhere else. Few choose the hard road now.” It steadies. “This once, the wood does not test you with a lie. It only asks you to choose, knowing what each road is. Choose with your eyes open, traveler — that clear seeing is its own gold, and you have earned it.”
scenes.prompt: Which way do you take — the gentle right, or the rugged straight?

choices.label: Bear right — the gentle path
choices.text: You take the easy right-hand way, and the ground stays kind beneath your feet, winding level through the trees. “Wisely weighed,” the moth says. “There is no shame in the gentler road — only know it keeps to the high ground, and the things that live in the low places, it never meets. You chose, and you knew what you chose: that understanding is the second gold.” It settles in you, cool and certain, like a coin pressed into the palm.

choices.label: Go straight on — the rugged path
choices.text: You set your face to the steeper, stonier way, the one that drops into the dark hollow. “The hard road,” the moth says, and there is real respect in it. “Few choose it; fewer still with open eyes. That seeing — choosing the harder true thing over the easy one — that is the second gold, and you have it now.” Then, lower: “Come. Mind your feet. It falls away just ahead, and his flies will find us in the low ground.”

scenes.text:
The path forks at a leaning post, and the blue light is already waiting — but it does not flee from you, and it does not lure. It drifts close, and it speaks your name, softly, as though it has known you a long time.

“There you are. I have been watching you since the fox. You let him die — no, no, don’t flinch from it; it was honest. Why should you starve for a dying king and his dying wood? They sent you to spend yourself for them, child, the way they spent all the others whose bones lie just there.” The light warms, kind as a hearth. “I am Raggeth. Take my mark, and the rot will never touch you. Walk my wood untouched, while it lasts — and it will not last. The crown is going out. Be on the winning side of the dark.”

The moth on your shoulder has gone very still, and very afraid.
scenes.prompt: Refuse the mark, or accept it?

choices.label: Refuse the mark
choices.text: “No,” you say, before you can talk yourself out of it. The warmth goes out of the light all at once. “A pity,” says Raggeth, not unkindly. “Then you walk hunted. No fox. No friends. Only me, behind every tree, until the wood is mine.” The light withdraws, and you are alone in a way you have never been alone. There at the fork the second golden cap gleams; you take it with a steady hand. You are unmarked, unbroken — and entirely on your own. “Cleverness,” the moth whispers, the only voice left to you, “and the harder courage of being alone. Now — right. Always right.”

choices.label: Accept the mark
choices.text: You hold out your hand. Raggeth lays a cap in it — not gold, but a cold black thing, slick as a drowned mushroom, and it does not warm to your skin; your skin cools to it. On your shoulder the moth recoils, its light shrinking from you as from a flame turned wrong. And the wood — the wood looks different now. The dead in their cold ground look like enemies. The dying king looks like a fool who would not let go. The rot looks almost beautiful. “Good,” Raggeth breathes. “Walk on, my own. Go right — there is nothing on the straight road for you now but bones, and you are past needing those.” The second golden cap lies in the moss; you pocket it without quite knowing why you still want it.

scenes.text:
The trees give way to a small graveyard — a dozen old stones, leaning every which way in the grey light. These are the king’s knights, the last of the old mushroom-guard, who stood against Raggeth an age ago and fell to the last, and were never avenged. The wood forgot them. The rot has not — it creeps among the stones like spilled ink.

At the center stands one great cracked stone, and at its foot a candle, long gone cold. “The last cap is here,” the moth breathes, “in the keeping of the dead. They will not give it to the timid. You must wake their captain — and you must not look away when he wakes.”
scenes.prompt: Light the candle and wake the guardian, or tiptoe past?

choices.label: Light the candle
choices.text: Your hands shake so badly you can barely breathe on the wick — but it catches, one small gold flame in a sea of grey. The great stone splits. Something rises from it: a knight of blackened oak and toadstool, vast, its eyes two coals, an age of grief in its ruined face. It would be so easy to run. You do not run. For a long, cold moment the dead captain weighs you — then slowly bows. “Courage,” it says, in a voice like a closing tomb, “is the last gold, and it is bought with fear, not the lack of it.” It lays the third cap in your hand, and then it does not sink back. It takes up its broken sword and falls in at your shoulder. “We could not save the king. We will see you to him. And when you face Raggeth — for you will — we will not look away, and neither will you.” You walk on with a dead knight at your side.

choices.label: Tiptoe quietly past
choices.text: You cannot do it. You hold your breath and slip between the graves, quiet as the dead themselves, and you do not light the candle, and you do not wake the captain. The last cap you find at the graveyard’s edge, set upon a small stone — a young knight’s grave, one who fell too soon. You lift it with hands that will not stop shaking, and all across that little ground you feel the weight of eyes that hoped for more from you, and let you pass anyway. No knight rises to walk with you. But the fox is still ahead, and the moth is still at your shoulder, and that will have to be enough.

scenes.text:
The graveyard of the old mushroom-guard — the dead who fell resisting Raggeth, an age ago, and were never avenged. You feel them notice you the moment you step in. Not the cap on the stones: the cap in your pocket, the cold black one, and the chill of it spreading up your arm. The rot does not touch you now. The dead see exactly why.

The great cracked stone splits without a candle. The captain rises, two coals for eyes, and looks at the mark on you with something worse than anger — recognition. “We died to keep this from spreading,” it says, “and here it walks in wearing a child’s face.” It lifts the cold dead candle from the stone and holds it out to you. “This is the cure, and it is cruel. Light it, and it will burn the dark out of you — it will hurt like a little dying. Or keep your master’s gift, and go to the pond to take the crown for him, and we will not stop you, because you are already lost.”
scenes.prompt: Light the candle and burn the mark away, or refuse it?

choices.label: Light it — burn the mark away
choices.text: You touch the flame to the wick, and the cold black cap in your pocket catches like dry leaves, and it burns — through your hand, up your arm, into the place where Raggeth had begun to make a home. It is a little death. You go down on the cold ground and you come back up scarred, and shaking, and yourself again. The Cap of Courage is in your hand; you do not remember the captain placing it there. “Courage,” it says, quieter now, “is bought with fear — and sometimes with worse. You nearly became what we died fighting. You turned back from it. Few do.” The mark is gone. The scar will not be.

choices.label: Refuse it — turn on the dead
choices.text: You close your hand over your pocket, over the cold cap, and you back away from the candle and its cruel little fire. “Then take your courage and your curse together,” the captain says, and there is no anger left in it, only a vast tiredness. The third cap it sets on the nearest stone; you take it, because some part of you still counts to three. The dead sink down and do not watch you go. The mark has the whole of you now. The wood ahead looks like spoils. You climb toward the pond to take the crown — and you know, without being told, who you mean to give it to.

scenes.text:
The graveyard of the old mushroom-guard — the dead who stood against Raggeth and fell, and were never avenged. You come among them alone, hunted, unmarked, the corpse-light’s refusal still cold in your chest.

The great cracked stone splits without a candle, and the captain rises, two coals for eyes — and looks at you a long moment, and slowly bows. “We know what you turned down at the fork,” it says, in a voice like a closing tomb. “He offered you the easy road and you spat on it, and you have walked alone ever since. That is its own courage — the cold kind, the kind with no one watching.” It lays the third cap in your hand. “We cannot walk with you; we are bound to this ground. But you have earned this clean. Go to the pond unbroken. Few reach it so.” The dead sink back. You are still alone — but you carry all three caps, and you carry them as your own.

wp6.title: The Way to the Pond
wp6.text:
Three caps, cold in your hand, and the wood gone nearly black around you. The moth’s light is a dying ember now; it can barely lift from your shoulder. The bell — the king’s heart — tolls once more, so faint you feel it more than hear it, and the silence that follows runs on too long before the next.

“Hurry,” the moth breathes. “He is almost gone. The path climbs from here — the pond lies above us, at the top of the wood, where the forest was born, and where, tonight, it may die.” The signpost points the way up into the dark. You climb.

scenes.text: You’ve chosen the hard way, and the moth knows it — its light bobs close, a little anxious. “The stony path,” it says. “Steeper, and longer, and the king’s old friends keep to it. Few come this way now.” Ahead the trail tips downward, dropping between the trees into the hollow below. And already the flies have found you — Raggeth’s flies, the same the moth warned of at the wood’s edge: small and black and stinging, whining at your ears, fretting at you to turn back. “Pay them no mind,” the moth says. “They cannot turn you unless you let them.”
scenes.prompt: Stride on boldly, or pick your way careful?

choices.label: Stride on boldly
choices.text: You set your jaw and go, swatting as you descend; the flies scatter and regroup, but you’ve shown them you won’t be turned. The moth’s light steadies.

choices.label: Pick your way careful
choices.text: You go slow and sure down the dropping path, watching your feet on the roots and stones. The flies pester, but you keep your footing and your patience.

scenes.text: [PAWN — not yet written. The Pawn’s Road version of the rugged arm (the marked / defiant walker on the stony path) is still to be drafted. Placeholder so the trail does not dead-end.]

The path bottoms out in a low, wet hollow, and here the flies are a torment — a thick whining cloud of them rising from the damp to swarm your face and hands, biting now, in earnest. This is their country. “His minions,” the moth says grimly, batting at them. “He keeps them thickest in the low places, where the rot pools. They want you to run back up the hill. Don’t.” The trail bends away to your right, climbing toward drier ground.
scenes.prompt: How do you face the swarm?

choices.label: Swat through and press on
choices.text: You duck your head and push right through the worst of it, fast, until the ground rises and the cloud thins behind you. “Good,” breathes the moth. “He’ll know you’re not so easily sent home.”

choices.label: Cover up and push slow
choices.text: You shield your face and walk steady through without panic, bearing right and up until they fall away. “Steady,” the moth says. “That’s its own kind of brave.”

choices.label: Falter — nearly turn back
choices.text: For a moment the biting is too much and you turn to flee up the hill — then catch yourself, grit your teeth, and force onward, shaken. The flies got their hooks in your nerve a little. You go on anyway.

scenes.text: [PAWN — not yet written. Rugged arm, Post 2. Placeholder so the trail does not dead-end.]

The path levels, and the air changes — cooler, green, resinous. These are the only pines in all the wood, and they are not sick; the rot has not come here. Just off the path, among their roots, an underground spring surfaces and bubbles up into a small clear pool, babbling to itself. And one pine creaks — a long, slow, talking sort of creak, the way no wind makes a tree sound. “Go to the water,” the moth whispers. “Step off the path, just here. This is the fairy’s spring, and it feeds the king’s own heart-well at the pond. The last clean magic in the wood. Be courteous.”

You kneel at the pool. The creaking pine bends low, and a voice comes out of it — tiny, ancient, dry as a hinge. “A traveler. On the king’s errand, and brave enough for the stony road. Few are, now.” The water is the clearest thing you’ve seen all night.
scenes.prompt: How do you take the fairy’s water?

choices.label: Kneel and ask her leave
choices.text: “May I carry some of your water?” you ask. The pine creaks, pleased. “Manners, even now. Take it — and take this with it.” She fills your flask with true spring-water, cold and bright, and leans close: “When you stand before the dark one’s pot, remember — the rot is drowned where the king’s gold meets the true water. Pour what I have given you. The dark cannot abide the clean.” You carry her water and her words.

choices.label: Cup your hands, drink, then fill quietly
choices.text: You drink first — so cold it aches, so clean it steadies you — then fill your flask. The fairy creaks softly, neither pleased nor cross. “Thirsty thing. You’ll need it more than you know before the night’s done. Mind you don’t waste it.” You have her water, but only a riddle, not the answer.

choices.label: Just fill your flask and hurry on
choices.text: You fill quickly and turn back to the path, the errand pressing on you. The pine’s creak falls silent behind you — you didn’t stop to listen. You carry the water without knowing what it’s for.

scenes.text: [PAWN — not yet written. Rugged arm, the Fairy Spring. The marked walker treats the fairy differently; to be drafted. Placeholder so the trail does not dead-end.]

The path runs flat and quiet — and then you’re among them. Faces. Not one or two now but a whole grove, faces in every trunk, eyes and mouths and old carved brows crowded close on every side. This is the heart of the watching wood. On the way in they were silent and shut-eyed — but here, near the spring’s clean magic, some are stirring. Eyes open as you pass. They are looking at you. “They know you carry the king’s gold,” the moth breathes. “They’re deciding what they make of you.”
scenes.prompt: How do you face the grove?

choices.label: Meet their eyes
choices.text: You stop and look back at all those old wooden eyes, and you do not flinch. A long creaking murmur passes trunk to trunk, like a held breath let go. “A friend of the king,” they sigh, in many voices. “Go on, and carry our last strength with you.” It settles on you like a warm cloak.

choices.label: Bow to them
choices.text: You bow your head to the watching faces, in respect for what they’ve guarded so long. The murmur is gentler, almost grateful. “Courteous, and kind. Go with our strength.”

choices.label: Hurry quietly past
choices.text: The crowd of waking faces is too much; you drop your eyes and walk through quick and quiet. They watch you go and say nothing. You feel them at your back a long while. No blessing, and no harm.

scenes.text: [PAWN — not yet written. Rugged arm, the Tree-Face Grove. The grove judges the marked walker differently; to be drafted. Placeholder so the trail does not dead-end.]

And here the ground rears up. The flat ends and the trail climbs — steep, stony, dark — up and up toward where the pond must be. This is the last and hardest stretch of the rugged road, and your legs already ache. “The king is just above,” the moth says, light straining upward. “But the wood asks one more thing of you here, where the brave are made: it asks whether you’ll climb. Courage is not the lack of weariness, traveler. It is climbing anyway.”
scenes.prompt: How do you take the hill?

choices.label: Dig in and climb hard
choices.text: You set your hands to the cold stone and haul yourself up, breath ragged, refusing to stop, until the slope gives way and you crest the top. Something in you has hardened to gold on the way up. “There,” the moth says, proud. “The last gold. You climbed.”

choices.label: Rest, then climb
choices.text: You catch your breath, steady your heart — then climb, slow and stubborn, all the way up without turning back. “Not the fastest,” says the moth, “but you did not quit. That is the gold.”

choices.label: Nearly turn back, then climb anyway
choices.text: Halfway up, the climb and the long night nearly beat you, and you almost turn for home — but you don’t. You crawl the last of it on will alone and stand, shaking, at the top. You know exactly what this gold cost.

scenes.text: [PAWN — not yet written. Rugged arm, the Steep Incline (Cap of Courage). Placeholder so the trail does not dead-end.]

wp7.title: The Pond
wp7.text: The climb brings you out at the pond — the old heart-well of the forest, whose waters rise and fall with the king’s own life.

seasonalIntro.text: The water lies black and brimming and still — yet no stars float in it, for the sky itself has gone dark. “The last of the king’s strength,” the moth murmurs, “pooled here, and waiting, while it holds.”

Where deep water should be there is only a cracked and shrinking hollow, a last puddle sinking into mud. “The pond drains as the king does,” the moth breathes. “Nearly empty now. We are nearly too late.”

scenes.textCont: You kneel at the king’s toadstool throne and show him the three golden caps — kindness, cleverness, courage, gathered the length of the wood. The dim old eyes find them, and something like dawn moves across his ruined face. “All three. Then you have already done a brave and a great thing — and what comes next is yours to choose.” His cracked hand lifts. “Set these in my crown now, and I am saved: the rot will heal, and you may go home in honor, your task done. No one could ask more of you.” His voice drops. “But know this before you choose. Raggeth still lives, deep in the wood, and he holds the heart of my crown — the last and truest gold. Save me now, and you save me for your lifetime. End him, and you save this wood forever. There is no shame in either road.”
scenes.prompt: Rest your quest here with honor, or go on to end Raggeth forever?

choices.label: Set the caps in the crown — your task is done
Keep the caps, and go end Raggeth forever
choices.text: “Then keep the gold,” the king says. “You’ll need it for what waits.” The moth flutters down before your face, its small light trembling. “This is where I must leave you. I cannot go where he is — his dark would snuff me out in a breath, and then you’d have no light at all. You go alone from here.” It rests a moment against your cheek, light as ash. “It is another twenty minutes’ walk to his hut, deep in the wood — but there are places to sit and rest along the way, and much to see, for the deep wood is terrible and beautiful both. Follow the red tree-arrows, and only them. You’ll see his hut across the hollow before the path reaches it; never leave the markers to go straight to it — the wood between is where the bones are. Stay on the path, and it will bring you to him.” The light lifts away. “Go bravely. And come back.” And then the moth is gone, and for the first time all night, you are alone.

endingVariants.text: One by one you press the golden caps home into the bare ring of the crown, and light runs through it and steadies the king — but you flinched, once, on the way here, when it counted, and the ending is a quieter one. The king lives; the wood will live. No retinue of friends comes to walk you out; the moth lights you to the road, faithful to the last, and that is enough, and it is a little lonely. “You saved my forest,” the king says, gentler than a bell. “Go home in honor — and be a little braver next time. There is always a next time, in a wood.” The face-trees open their eyes as you pass, and watch you go, and do not quite smile. Your story is complete.

One by one you press the golden caps home into the bare ring of the king’s crown — and the moment the third is set, light runs through it like dawn through water, and does not stop. It pours from the crown into the king, into the throne, into the roots, out through the whole black wood. King Bolete straightens, grey going green, his crown blazing gold; the rot draws back into the earth; and all around the pond, the dying simply stops. The heart-well answers him, its waters clearing and rising. The king stands — tall, and shining, and saved — and his voice is no longer a whisper but a bell: “You carried my crown out of the dark and made me whole. Go home in honor, brave one. The wood will sing your name.” As you walk back down through the trees, the forest is already waking around you — green returning, birdsong, the face-trees opening their eyes to watch you pass and, one by one, beginning to smile. You saved the king. You saved the forest. Your story is complete.

Far off in the deep wood a thin green smoke still rises — Raggeth, unbeaten, biding. But that is a tale for another brave soul, another day. Tonight, you have won.

scenes.textCont: On a toadstool throne at the water’s edge sits King Bolete — grey to the bone, cracked like old wood, his crown a bare dark ring. “You came,” he breathes, and then he sees the cold thing in you, and his failing eyes close. “Ah. So that is how it is.” You carry his three caps. You do not kneel to mend them. The mark in you knows another use for a crown.
scenes.prompt: Where do you carry the crown?

choices.label: Into the deep wood — to Raggeth
Out of the wood, the way you came

exits.label: Accept the dark — THE END
exits.reveal: You carry the crown down into the deep wood and set the caps yourself into the cold ring, and they wake the wrong way — a black light, a crown for the dark one. Raggeth takes it from your hands almost tenderly. “My herald,” he says. You turn, and the wood goes out behind you, root to root, the face-trees’ eyes closing one last time. The king’s heart stops between one silence and the next. You walk at the dark one’s side now, wearing your own face, and you do not remember why that should trouble you.

exits.label: The wood grants one last mercy — flee
exits.reveal: Something stops your hand on the cold ring — the memory of a silver eye, maybe, or the moth’s small light guttering one final time at the very edge of you. You drop the crown and you run. The trees, dying, part for you anyway — one last kindness from a wood you betrayed — and spit you out into grey daylight at the road’s edge, shaking, empty-handed, alive. Behind you the forest falls dark. But your feet are on the road, and they are still yours, and they carry you home.

endingVariants.text: [DRAFT — Pawn’s Road, fallen. You bear the king’s caps down into the deep wood, toward the one whose mark you wear.]

exits.label: Accept the dark — THE END
exits.reveal: You bear the crown out of the wood the way you came in — but it is no rescue you carry it to. Raggeth is waiting at the tree-line as though he always was, and you set the golden caps into the cold ring and crown him with your own two hands, there in the last of the daylight. The forest dies behind you both, quietly, completely. He keeps you. You wear your own face still, which is the cruelest part, and you have quite forgotten there was ever anything wrong with that.

exits.label: The wood grants one last mercy — flee
exits.reveal: At the very tree-line, with the cold ring in your hands, you stop. You think of the fox you let die, and for the first time it is unbearable. You let the crown fall in the leaves and you run — out of the wood, into the grey ordinary light of the road, empty-handed and shaking and free. The forest goes dark behind you. You could not save it. You saved the last small part of yourself, and some nights that will have to be enough.

endingVariants.text: [DRAFT — Pawn’s Road, fallen. You carry the king’s caps back out of the wood — but not to safety.]

scenes.textCont: On a toadstool throne at the water’s edge sits King Bolete — grey to the bone, cracked like old wood, the mushrooms of his crown wilted brown. “You came,” he breathes. “And you came back to yourself along the way; I can see the scar of it. That is harder than never falling.” You kneel at the throne, and you set the three golden caps home into the bare ring of the crown. Light wakes in it — thinner than the bright roads, but true. “Now choose,” the king says. “Which way will you carry what you’ve mended?”
scenes.prompt: Choose your way from the pond.

choices.label: Out of the wood, the short way home
On into the deep wood, to face Raggeth

endingVariants.text: You mend the crown alone, as you did everything else since the fork — no fox, no knight, no mark, only your own two unbroken hands. The king lives; the wood will live; and no friends come from the shadows to thank you, because you made none, and you asked for none. You walk out into a cold and lonely dusk, unbroken, unbowed, unthanked. “You never sold yourself,” the king says quietly, “though I think he offered you the world. Some walkers I remember for their friends. You, I will remember for your spine.”

You go down into the deep wood with the mended crown and the burn of the cure still raw in you, and you face Raggeth wearing the scar where his mark used to be. He knows you. “You were nearly mine,” he says, almost wounded. “I was,” you answer, “and I came back.” That is the thing he cannot abide, and it is the thing that breaks him. The wood is saved. You carry the scar of what you almost became out of the dark with you, and you will carry it always. “You mended more than a crown tonight,” the king says. “Be gentle with the place it healed.”

You take the short way out, the mended crown behind you and the king’s heart beating again, and you walk home hollowed out by how close it was — how near you came to carrying that same crown to the dark one instead. The wood will live. You saved it, barely, and the barely is what stays with you. “You came back from the edge of yourself,” the king says, “and that is no small mending. Go easy. The hollow fills again, in time, if you let it.”

rg_road.title: Into the Deep Wood
rg_road.text: You cross from the pond and the red markers take you down into the deep wood — darker here than anywhere, no moth, no king, no fox, only you and the red arrows nailed to the black trees, one and then the next. The dark does not last. The trees begin to thin, the ground rises in a long, gentle slope, and the path climbs you up, out of the gloom, into sudden startling light —

rg_meadow.title: The Wildflower Meadow
rg_meadow.text:
— a meadow. A wide, sunlit meadow, deep in wildflowers, warm and gold and humming with bees, the loveliest thing you have seen in all this long dark night. After so much rot and cold it is almost too much; it is almost too lovely, here, so near the dark one’s house. And a voice you know drifts sweet across the flowers — Raggeth’s, but soft now, kind now, nothing like the cold thing in the wood. “There now. Isn’t this better? You’ve come so far, little one. You’re so tired. Sit a while. Rest. The king has waited this long; he can wait a little more.” There are benches here, set among the flowers, and they look so inviting.

The path leads on through the flowers to a quiet picnic place, tables and benches in the warm gold light, and the pull to stop is strong — stronger than the flies ever were. This is the wood’s last trick, and the craftiest: the flies tried to scare you back; the meadow tries to keep you. Sit, it murmurs. Stay. Forget the cold king and the cold wood. Why walk on to something so frightening, when here it is so warm?
rg_meadow.prompt: Rest a moment, then rise — or refuse to stop at all?

choices.label: Rest a moment, then rise and walk on
choices.text: You let yourself sit — your legs have earned it, and a brave heart is no good exhausted. You breathe the warm air, you feel the sun. And then you stand up, because you remember the king’s grey face and the dying wood, and no meadow, however lovely, will make you forget it. The warmth claws at you to stay — and you walk on anyway. Behind you, Raggeth’s sweet voice curdles. Resting was wise; rising was braver.

choices.label: Refuse to stop — march straight through
choices.text: You don’t trust the warmth for a moment. You keep your eyes on the red arrows and march straight through the flowers without sitting, without slowing, and the meadow’s sweetness sours behind you as it fails to hold you. Hard, and unfooled — though you’ll reach the lair more tired.

rg_grove2.title: The Second Grove
rg_grove2.text: The meadow ends, the light dies behind you, and the trees close in once more — and you come into a second grove of the face-trees, the watching faces, deeper and older and graver than the first. These are the last of the forest before the dark one’s ground, and they are afraid for you. Eyes open all around; mouths work in the bark. “Turn back,” some of them whisper. “No one who goes on comes back the same.” But others — the oldest, the bravest — only look at you steadily, and say: “If anyone can, it is the one who came this far. Go on. We will hold the light at your back as long as we can.”
rg_grove2.prompt: How do you take the grove’s last word?

choices.label: Promise them you’ll end it
choices.text: You set your hand to the nearest old face and promise: you’ll free the wood, or fall trying. The grove sighs, a long sound like wind though there is no wind, and their fear eases into something like hope. They are with you now, all of them, as far as they can go.

choices.label: Thank them, and walk on quietly
choices.text: You bow your head to the watching faces, say nothing, and walk on into the dark. They watch you go in silence, and the silence follows you a long way.

rg_lair.title: The Lair in Sight
rg_lair.text: And then, through a gap in the black trees, you see it: across a hollow, a little black hut, crooked as a witch’s, and before it a great black cauldron with sick green smoke crawling up. It looks so close. The path does not go toward it — it bends away, the long way round. And the cold voice is back, the kind warmth all gone now: “Why walk so far, little traveler? The hut is just there. Cut across; save your legs. Come straight to me.” It is Raggeth. The wood between you and the hut is still, and waiting. But you remember the bones, the corpse-light, the moth’s last warning. The red markers go the long way for a reason.
rg_lair.prompt: Stay on the path, or cut across?

choices.label: Stay on the red markers
choices.text: You don’t leave the path, though the voice wheedles and the hut sits there tempting the whole way round. The arrows lead you safe, down and around, and Raggeth’s voice sours from coaxing to a hiss as he sees you won’t be tricked.

choices.label: Cut across toward the hut
choices.text: You step off the markers toward the close, easy hut — and the ground is not ground. The dark between the trees is the bone-field; it drags at your feet, the flies rise in a black roar, and the corpse-light kindles ahead, smiling. This is how he takes travelers. The wood has you — but not yet.

rg_hut.title: The Hut and the Cauldron
rg_hut.buildNote: REAL-WORLD: put a physical 'KEEP CLOSED' sign on the actual hut hatch — there may be real wasps in there.
rg_hut.text: The red markers bring you, at last, the long way round, to the hut itself. Up close it’s small and mean and very old, its black boards weeping the same rot that’s killing the wood. The cauldron stands before it, taller than you, full of a slow green boil — and all at once you understand: this is the wound. This is where the rot is made. Raggeth is here, though you can’t quite see him — a thinness in the air, a cold, a voice. “So. The king’s little errand-runner. Come all this way.” On the hut’s face is a small black hatch, and the voice turns silky. “There’s a treasure behind that hatch, you know. The king’s last gold, perhaps. Open it. Go on — open it, and see.”
rg_hut.prompt: Open the hatch, or leave it?

choices.label: Leave the hatch shut
choices.text: You don’t touch it. The answer was never behind a door he wants you to open. Raggeth’s voice curdles with annoyance. The cauldron. It was always the cauldron.

choices.label: Open the hatch
choices.advanceLabel: Leave the hatch shut — back away
choices.text: Your hand goes to the latch — and a night’s worth of warnings catch you a beat too late: the hatch is not where the answer is. It’s where his swarm is. His swarm — get back!

rg_cauldron.title: The Cauldron
rg_cauldron.buildNote: Escalating cauldron hint text below is DRAFT placeholder — owner to finalize (per the script's 'what's left to write').
rg_cauldron.text:
The rot is brewed here, and it cannot be fought — only unmade. You have the king’s three golden caps, warm in your pocket: kindness, cleverness, courage. You understand what you must do — give them to the cauldron, the king’s gold cast into the dark’s own pot.

One by one you drop them in: Kindness. Cleverness. Courage. The green boil shudders; light fights dark in the pot. But it is not enough — the rot rises to swallow the gold, and Raggeth laughs. “Gold in my pot? It’ll be black gold by morning.” The caps are drowning. You must quench the rot — drown it first. With what?

scenes.prompt: Quench the rot. What do you do?

choices.label: Pour the fairy’s spring-water into the cauldron
Cast another handful of gold after the caps
hints: The cauldron flares green and furious and the gold sinks deeper. “More gold?” Raggeth purrs. “Feed me all you like.” The wood darkens a notch. At your hip, the fairy’s flask sloshes, cold and patient.
It flares again, higher, beating you back with its heat. Gold is not the answer — the fairy told you the answer. The clean water. Pour it.

choices.label: Strike the cauldron over
hints: You heave at it and it will not budge, and the rot laps higher up the gold. Not force. Remember her words: the rot is drowned where the king’s gold meets the true water. Your flask.

endingVariants.text: You lift the fairy’s flask and pour the clean spring-water into the cauldron — the king’s gold meeting the true water, exactly as she told you — and the cauldron screams, a long, cracking, world-ending sound, and splits from rim to foot. The green rot pours out into the ground and is gone, drunk down by a starving earth. And Raggeth — the thinness in the air, the cold, the dry voice — comes apart with his pot, unraveling like smoke in a wind, with one last astonished sigh, into nothing. And you are not alone after all: the grove’s strength is in you, and far off you hear the face-trees waking, every one, eyes opening across the whole wood. The hut sags into ruin, and from the cauldron’s wreck you lift the last and truest gold: the heart of the king’s crown. You carry it home through a forest coming back to life; at the castle you set it in its place, and King Bolete rises whole and shining, and the long night ends in a blaze of dawn. The forest is reborn, and it will not forget the one who saved it.

scenes.prompt: Quench the rot. What do you do?

choices.label: Pour the water from the fairy’s flask into the cauldron
Cast another cap into the pot
hints: It flares; the gold sinks. That isn’t it. What else did you carry out of that green, clean place by the pines?
Higher, hotter, the rot nearly over the gold now. The flask at your hip — the cold spring-water. You never knew what it was for. Maybe this is it. Pour it.

choices.label: Plunge your hands in to snatch the caps back
hints: You jerk back before the boiling green takes your hands. Not that. Think — the cleanest thing you touched all night was the fairy’s spring. The water in your flask. Pour it in.

scenes.prompt: You have no clean water. What do you do?

choices.label: Force the king’s light down into the rot with everything you have left
Cast another cap into the pot
hints: It flares and gives you nothing; the gold sinks. There is no clean water in your hands — you never knelt at the spring on the stony road. There is only the gold, and you, and everything the road made of you. If it is to be done, your own will must do it.
The rot is nearly over the gold. No gift will save it now. Only you. Set your teeth and force the king’s light down — drive it into the dark by main strength, whatever it costs.

endingVariants.text: You have no clean water — only the king’s gold, your own two hands, and everything the long road made of you. You set your teeth and force the king’s light down into the rot by sheer will — and the grove’s last strength is in you, and steadies the breaking just enough — fierce, and costly, and not clean. The cauldron cracks, an ugly, grinding break, and the backlash throws you to the ground. The rot drains away; Raggeth comes apart with a furious wail; the wood will live. But it cost. You rise slow and lift the heart of the crown from the wreck with shaking hands, and walk home aching — and you’ll always know the dawn came a little dimmer than it might have, that there was a cleaner way through the wood you never found. Still: you faced the dark alone, and you did not break, and the king lives because you climbed. That is no small thing.
